description: A low evergreen dwarf shrub 10-40 cm tall of wiry, woody stems densely clothed in tiny, scale-like leaves in four rows, the plant of Norway's coastal heaths. In August and September it flowers in spikes of small pale purple bells, and in winter the heath turns bronze-brown.

season_notes.winter: Bronze and rusty brown, under snow or wet and bare in the mild coast winters; the spent flower spikes grey.
season_notes.spring: Dull green as the shoots begin to grow in May and June.
season_notes.summer: Dark green; the flower spikes open pale purple in late summer, loud with bumblebees.
season_notes.fall: Flowering into September, then the spikes brown; ptarmigan feed on the shoots.

notes: Grown from Mertens' mountain heather, the library's Ericaceae dwarf shrub with tiny appressed leaves, as a larger, darker, bronze-wintering hummock. COMPROMISES: the leaves are scale-like and overlapping in four rows (decussate); the generator has only flat leaf shapes, so they are 3 mm 'lanceolate' leaves on the template's dense cards, which reads as a fine dark texture; the flower spikes are 'candle' flowers. The tree generator grows each plant as a separate hummock: continuous heath carpet (as Lofoten has) would want a ground-layer form (shrubfield or a dense patch), not individual shrubs. Ling heath is a fire- and grazing-maintained cultural landscape on the Norwegian coast (lyngbrenning, the old practice of burning heath): the heaths of Lofoten are partly of that origin. Heights, colours and phenology are the drafter's knowledge (no source read beyond the GBIF name check); willow and rock ptarmigan eating the shoots and red deer browsing it in winter, likewise. Lofoten's calendar: polar night in December and early January, birch bare from about October to the end of May, leaf-out in late May and June, autumn yellow in September; the climate is oceanic, winters mild for the latitude, the treeline low (a few hundred metres) under salt wind.
